title: Convergence and the Gibbs Phenomenon
intro: Adding harmonics brings the sum closer to the signal, but how fast depends on how smooth the signal is. Next to a jump the sum overshoots by about 9% of the jump, and no number of harmonics will remove that overshoot; at the jump itself the sum settles on the midpoint.

blocks.text: The series for a square wave and for a triangle wave use the same odd harmonics, yet the triangle is accurate with a handful of them while the square wave is still visibly ragged at forty. The difference lies in how quickly the coefficients fall. From the Fourier Series: Building a Wave (#/math/fourier-transform/fourier-series) page: the square wave has $A_k = 4/(\pi k)$, the triangle $A_k = 8/(\pi^2k^2)$. Compare the two at a few harmonics:

Multiplying the harmonic number by 11 (from 9 to 99) divides the square wave's coefficient by 11 but the triangle's by 121, which is $11^2$. These are the $1/k$ and $1/k^2$ laws. The rule behind them, for a periodic signal:

items: A signal with jumps has coefficients that fall like $1/k$.
A continuous signal whose slope jumps (corners) has coefficients that fall like $1/k^2$.
Each further derivative that stays continuous buys another factor of $1/k$. A signal with every derivative smooth has coefficients that fall faster than any power of $k$.

blocks.text: The reason is the differentiation rule from the series page: the coefficients of $x'$ are $jk\omega_0 c_k$. The derivative of a triangle is a square wave, whose coefficients fall like $1/k$; so $c_k$ of the triangle is that divided by $k$, hence $1/k^2$. A square wave's derivative is a train of impulses, whose coefficients do not fall at all, so $c_k \sim 1/k$. Each corner or jump in the signal is a sharp feature, and sharp features need high frequencies.
The consequences for the error are large. The RMS gap between a signal and its partial sum with harmonics $0 \ldots N$, for $N = 1, 3, 7, 15$ and 39:

The two with jumps roughly halve their error when $N$ is multiplied by four or five (an error falling like $1/\sqrt{N}$). The two with only corners do better still: their error falls by nearly a factor of 3 each time $N$ doubles (like $1/N^{3/2}$, since the squared error is the tail of a sum of $1/k^4$). To get the square wave's RMS gap under 0.1 takes harmonics up to $k = 41$ (the gap is 0.0982 there, against 0.1006 at 39); the triangle is already under 0.1 with the fundamental alone, $N = 1$.

Look at where the square wave's sum goes wrong. Away from the jumps the sum hugs the signal ever more tightly; at $N = 39$ the largest error between $t = 0.1$ and $t = 0.4$ (a plateau) is $0.027$. Near the jump it behaves quite differently. A partial sum cannot jump: it is a finite sum of smooth waves. To get from $-1$ up to $+1$ across a narrow gap it has to move fast, and it overshoots on the way, then rings back. The height of the highest peak of the sum for the square wave (jump size 2) is

The peak does not shrink to 1. It settles toward 1.1790. That excess of 0.1790 is $8.95\%$ of the jump of 2, and it is the Gibbs phenomenon, after J. Willard Gibbs, who explained it in 1899 (Henry Wilbraham had found it in 1848). The overshoot gets narrower as $N$ grows, and its position crowds in toward the jump, at $t = T/(2(N+1))$ after it. For $N = 7$ that is $T/16 = 0.0625$ s when $T = 1$. But the height stays put: more harmonics squeeze the overshoot into a narrower region beside the jump without lowering it. In the limit the sum converges to the signal at every point where the signal is continuous. At the jump itself it converges to the midpoint of the two one-sided limits: every partial sum of the square wave passes through 0 at $t = 0$, halfway between $-1$ and $+1$, whatever value you assign the signal there. And the convergence is not uniform near a jump: however large $N$ is, there are points just beside it where the sum is still about 9% of the jump away from the signal. The horn of the overshoot slides in toward the jump and never goes away.

The 8.95% figure comes from an integral. Summing the square wave's series up to $k = N$ turns into an integral of $\sin u / u$, and its largest value is $\frac{2}{\pi}\operatorname{Si}(\pi) = \frac{2}{\pi}\times 1.8519 = 1.1790$, where $\operatorname{Si}(x) = \int_0^x \frac{\sin u}{u}\,du$. The number only depends on the sum's shape at a jump, so it is the same for any jump: for the sawtooth the sum overshoots the local value of the ramp (the ramp has reached 0.975 there when $N = 39$) by the same $0.179$, reaching 1.154, and for a jump of 5 volts the overshoot is $0.0895 \times 5 = 0.447$ V.

This matters in practice. A filter that keeps only the low harmonics of a sharp edge (a bandlimited channel, a brick-wall low-pass) will ring and overshoot by about 9% of the step, however wide you make the band. The remedy is not more bandwidth but a gentler edge: smoothing the jump, or tapering the coefficients with a window so that the sum stops chasing the corner. Both change the shape of the error, not the underlying fact that sharp features need high frequencies.

The view is from the front. With Harmonics added at 39 the dark sum follows the dashed square wave but has a horn above the top of each jump and a matching dip below; the readout says the RMS gap is 0.1006. Drag N down to 7 and the horns are wider and lower, but only slightly: their height is 1.1842 compared with 1.1792 at N = 39. Then change Input signal to triangle wave and the horns are gone, because a continuous signal has nothing to overshoot.

The full-wave rectified sine has corners but no jumps. At N = 3 the readout gives an RMS gap of 0.0197. Compare the spectrum bars: 0.424, 0.085, 0.036, 0.020 for $k = 1, 2, 3, 4$. They fall like $1/k^2$, so the harmonic at $k = 10$ is only 0.0032, less than one percent of the fundamental.

blocks.title: Predict the decay
blocks.text: For the full-wave rectified sine, $A_k = 4/(\pi(4k^2 - 1))$. How does $A_{10}$ compare with $A_1$?
solution: $A_1 = 4/(3\pi) = 0.4244$ and $A_{10} = 4/(399\pi) = 0.003191$. The ratio is $0.0075$. For a pure $1/k^2$ law the ratio would be $1/100 = 0.01$; the formula is $1/(4k^2 - 1)$, so the match improves as $k$ grows. So the coefficients fall as $1/k^2$: the signal has corners but no jumps.

blocks.title: How many harmonics?
blocks.text: The RMS gap for the square wave after harmonics up to $N$ is $\sqrt{1 - P_N}$ with $P_N = \frac{8}{\pi^2}\sum_{k\ \text{odd}\le N} 1/k^2$. Is $N = 39$ enough for a gap below 0.1?
solution: At $N = 39$ the partial power is 0.98987, so the gap is $\sqrt{0.01013} = 0.1006$, just above 0.1. At $N = 41$ the power is 0.99035 and the gap $\sqrt{0.00965} = 0.0982$. So you need $N = 41$, two more harmonics. The error only falls like $1/\sqrt N$, so each further digit of accuracy costs a hundred times as many harmonics.
blocks.answer: No: $N = 41$ is the first that gives a gap under 0.1.

blocks.title: Gibbs on a step
blocks.text: A band-limited channel passes only the first 39 harmonics of a $\pm 5$ V square wave. How high does the output peak?
solution: The unit square wave peaks at 1.1792, so with $\pm5$ V it peaks at $5 \times 1.1792 = 5.896$ V, an overshoot of 0.896 V, which is $8.96\%$ of the 10 V jump. Doubling the bandwidth to 79 harmonics would not change this meaningfully; the overshoot would be about 5.895 V.
blocks.answer: About 5.90 V, an overshoot near 9% of the 10 V jump.
